title: Trump's midterm campaign tour stops in Iowa
description: Trump's midterm campaign tour stops in Iowa   Republicans are facing a tough fight in Iowa. President Trump's campaign tour stopped in the state in ho
body:
Trump's midterm campaign tour stops in Iowa   Republicans are facing a tough fight in Iowa. President Trump's campaign tour stopped in the state in hopes of rallying voters.

    
        Politics
    


      
            
                  
            October 23, 20266:36 AM ET
         
      
       From
   
   
                              By                
      Sheila Brummer
  
            


      
      Trump's midterm campaign tour stops in Iowa
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6009838/nx-s1-9975539" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    




      Republicans are facing a tough fight in Iowa. President Trump's campaign tour stopped in the state in hopes of rallying voters.   


    
        
          Transcript
        
    A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:  President Trump is on a whirlwind tour to rally support for Republicans in competitive midterm races. Iowa Public Radio's Sheila Brummer reports from Sioux City, where he campaigned last night.SHEILA BRUMMER, BYLINE: A circus-like atmosphere outside a hangar at the Sioux Gateway Airport, where vendors sell all things Trump. Among them was Ricardo Boyles (ph) with his colorful hats.RICARDO BOYLES: I have them in black, camo, pink, blue, red, green.BRUMMER: Boyles left a Trump rally in Greenville, South Carolina, Tuesday night to make it to Iowa by Thursday.BOYLES: One thousand three hundred and thirty-one miles, 21 hours and 40 minutes. It was fun. I love the cornfields.BRUMMER: Local supporters included Robert Byrne (ph), who says he bleeds red when it comes to politics.ROBERT BYRNE: My vote will be for Republicans up and down the ballot, every bit of it, because, for some reason, the choice this year is between sanity and insanity.BRUMMER: This is friendly territory for the president.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Well, thank you very much. I love this place.BRUMMER: Here in Iowa's 4th Congressional District, registered Republicans outnumber Democrats by more than 2 to 1. But republicans face a tougher fight statewide. Congresswoman Ashley Hinson is running for Senate against Democrat Josh Turek. A new poll conducted for the Cook Political Report puts Turek 2 percentage points ahead within the poll's margin of error. Trump urged people to get behind Hinson.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)TRUMP: She will never let far-left maniacs push the radical left insanity on Iowa's children. She's...BRUMMER: Trump also called on voters to elect Republican Zach Lahn as governor, who faces Democrat Rob Sand, Iowa's state auditor. Polls gives Sand an 11-point lead. While speaking for more than 90 minutes, Trump mainly talked about himself, touting tax cuts, his international policies and support for farmers. He riled people up by bringing up transgender rights and another favorite topic, fake news, multiple times. He also returned to his false claims that he won in 2020, and that he should be able to run again because...(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)TRUMP: We won three times, but that's right. You know, I want the three wins, but I don't...BRUMMER: Trump plans to return to Iowa November 1, just two days before the midterms.For NPR News, I'm Sheila Brummer, Sioux City, Iowa.

title: Trump must sit for a deposition in his BBC defamation lawsuit, judge rules
description: A magistrate judge orders President Trump to sit for a deposition in a case he's brought against the BBC for defamation.
body:
A magistrate judge orders President Trump to sit for a deposition in a case he's brought against the BBC for defamation.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:  President Trump will have to sit for a deposition in a $10 billion defamation case he brought against the BBC.LEILA FADEL, HOST:  Yeah. A federal magistrate judge ruled Thursday that it was Trump's choice to sue the British broadcaster, and he has to play by the rules of the court or face sanctions.MARTÍNEZ: NPR media correspondent David Folkenflik attended the hearing in Miami. David, why was there even a question about whether the president would sit for a deposition?DAVID FOLKENFLIK, BYLINE: Well, I mean, he is the president. And it's this president - right? - A. You know, this was a - in some ways, a hearing about logistics in front of a magistrate judge. It sounds like it's a pretty pro forma kind of thing. But actually, you know, really fundamentally at its core is a question of whether the sitting president of the United States will submit to the will of a federal court. He had agreed to sit for a deposition, which is to say questions under oath, for last Friday, October 16, but it was canceled. President's legal team said it was due to matters of national importance and said he could do it sometime in January. There's a deadline in mid-December for the completion of what's called discovery. It's where the two sides get evidence for one another for this case.Trump's private attorney invoked the idea yesterday the president does a lot more things than you could possibly know. The BBC's lead attorney said, hey. That's fake news. He noted that last Friday, Trump campaigned with a Republican Senate candidate in Dalton, Georgia, then went to Mar-a-Lago for an event for the Republican National Committee. The magistrate judge said, no. Let's do this. You're going to have to do this by December 11. There's a possibility that could shift if the judge presiding over the case changes the deadline.And the judge also said, look. You got to hand over evidence. All the material that the president's legal team gave to the BBC was stuff that the BBC had either handed over to the president's team or that - stuff that the president's legal team, according to the BBC's lawyers, had pulled down from the internet. Not any private records at all. The judge said that strained credulity.MARTÍNEZ: All right. So tell us about the case.FOLKENFLIK: So back in October of 2024, just a few weeks before the presidential elections, the BBC show "Panorama" broadcast a documentary in which it spliced together parts of the January 6 speech, 2021, that made it seem as though Trump, at that, you know, pivotal day, when there was a siege of Congress - made it seem like he was bluntly calling for violence to prevent the certification of Joe Biden as the winner of that race. Trump says this was false, deceptive and defamatory under Florida law - is seeking $10 billion.He's tweaked a little bit the grounds on which he's doing it, putting aside the claim that he made initially that this damaged his business and future financial prospects. Now he's talking mostly about his reputational injury. But as the BBC argues, his reputation is bound up in business and politics. I want to point out to listeners, "Panorama" was not aired in Florida or on U.S. channels or on the BBC's, you know, streaming partners here in the U.S. And the other thing the BBC points out is Trump not only won the 2024 race. He won Florida, handily, too.MARTÍNEZ: What's the BBC hope to learn from Trump's testimony?FOLKENFLIK: The BBC did apologize for the splicing. It did - in fact, there was a fallout for some of its officials. But it's now trying to determine what his mindset was. Maybe they can show that he did want to encourage violence. They noted that a lot of defendants said Trump's speech had urged them on.MARTÍNEZ: Last thing, David. I mean, President Trump has sued lots of news organizations. What's the significance of this one?FOLKENFLIK: Well, you saw at the outset of his term that media outlets were settling - CBS and ABC. And he's sued, again as a private citizen, all kinds of news outlets, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, others. The BBC has been fighting back, going after details of January 6, but also going after potential vulnerability to the president. He doesn't really want his financial details public. And they are securing information about both the level of interest in people joining Mar-a-Lago, his resort, as members and what costs he has charged them over the years, in recent years since - has been able to charge them.Trump right now in this lawsuit has to decide how willing he is to play by the rules. Is he willing to submit to the rule of law in federal court in a lawsuit that he voluntarily brought? And if not, it looks very likely that this case will be dismissed.MARTÍNEZ: That's NPR media correspondent David Folkenflik. David, thanks.FOLKENFLIK: You bet.

title: At a Texas high school football game, fans offer a glimpse into evolving politics
description: We talk with voters at a Texas high school football game at the tailgate, in line at the concession booth and in the stands to hear about the i
body:
We talk with voters at a Texas high school football game at the tailgate, in line at the concession booth and in the stands to hear about the issues that matter to Texans this cycle.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  Texas and football - a classic combination no matter who you root for.(CHEERING)DETROW: Root for or vote for. Texas has been a safe Republican state for three decades, but polling suggests next month's midterms could be tight. So Houston Public Media's Bianca Seward takes us to the bleachers at Deer Park High School's homecoming game, where fans in this Houston suburb offer a glimpse into the state's changing politics.UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: Go go go.(CHEERING)BIANCA SEWARD, BYLINE: In Texas, the high school football field is sacred ground.ERIC SCHUTLZ: And it's a culture that, no matter if you're in big city or rural Texas, where I grew up, it's a time for everybody, just the same principle as going to church, right?SEWARD: That's Eric Schutlz. He and his wife and kids come every Friday night that they can.SCHUTLZ: It's kind of a function of the community and for families to get together - community - and support everybody - band, football players, cheerleaders.SEWARD: That's what brought Emily Taylor out to the game.EMILY TAYLOR: Sometimes I forget that there's a football game going on 'cause I'm only here for her. She's next after this.SEWARD: Taylor comes to watch her niece Sydney cheer on the sidelines.UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: Junior co-captain, two time All American - Sydney Wilber.TAYLOR: Let's go, Sydney.SEWARD: Taylor is a Democrat living in Deer Park, a conservative suburb of Houston. But she says something feels different this cycle.TAYLOR: The other day, I took some back roads, and I saw two houses that had Talarico and Gina Hinojosa signs outside. And it made me so hopeful because I do not remember seeing that during Kamala Harris' run.SEWARD: Recent polling supports Taylor's hunch. Democrats Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico have forced Governor Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton into competitive contests. Both races are effectively tied.TAYLOR: If we can do it, this is the year.UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: Deer Park, first down.SCHUTLZ: I figure it'll still stay red.SEWARD: When Eric Schutlz heads to the poll this year, he says he'll vote Republican with two specific groups of people on his mind.SCHUTLZ: You know, and at the end of the day, you know, kids and elderly are important, right? Elderly paved the way, kids are the future. So those are important topics that need to be taken care of.SEWARD: And despite all the talk of a tight race, he's not convinced the state will change parties this year.SCHUTLZ: The dividing line comes in bigger cities, but when you get in smaller communities, they're more like-minded. And, you know, I think it'll stay the same.SEWARD: Nate Esser, sitting a couple dozen bleachers down, is hoping Schutlz is wrong.NATE ESSER: I'm hoping people will wake up and realize that current administration is not doing anything for them right now.SEWARD: And Esser has a long list of concerns.ESSER: Inflation, the economy - I mean, my 401K is doing great, but, you know, that doesn't benefit most people. Yeah, gas prices, fairness to people, like, treating everyone fairly, equal rights for trans people, gay people, people of color. Like, I'm sick of this ICE crap.SEWARD: Immigration enforcement has taken center stage in political debates across Texas after a series of incidents involving ICE agents and allegations of excessive force. But still, Esser isn't sure many others in the Deer Park community agree with him.ESSER: You've interviewed a lot of people around here. And my guess is I'm one of the few that has spoken like this to you.SEWARD: I tell him it's actually been a mixed bag.ESSER: Really?SEWARD: Fifty/fifty.ESSER: Really? That's - that makes me feel good then. That surprises me, yeah.UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #3: What color (inaudible)?UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #4: Blue.UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #3: Blue. OK.STEPHANIE PETERSON: I need two chili cheese hot dogs.SEWARD: Stephanie Peterson manages the concession booth.PETERSON: Plain nachos.SEWARD: She makes sure the shelves stay stocked and keeps an eye on rising prices, both for the booth and for her own family's pantry.PETERSON: Just the prices going up, it's killing us. Basically, now you have to have two income family just to survive, and we don't have that. So it's like you don't know how you're going to survive anymore.SEWARD: In the fourth quarter of the election, for either party to win, they'll need all voters ready to jump off the bench. But Peterson, who voted for Trump in 2024, says she might stay home on Election Day.PETERSON: I don't know. It depends. I'm undecided. I'll just say that.SEWARD: From the economy to immigration, folks in the crowd have their own priorities, and they want very different outcomes on election day.UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: Touchdown Deer.(CHEERING)SEWARD: But as the game comes to a close, their voices blend into one, cheering together for the same team under the Friday night lights.For NPR News, I'm Bianca Seward in Deer Park, Texas.(SOUNDBITE OF HI-TEK SONG, "ALL I NEED IS YOU")

title: The Pentagon's guidelines for "responsible AI" aren't always followed, report shows
description: Three of the Pentagon projects surveyed
body:
Three of the Pentagon projects surveyed by GAO included weapons for counter-camouflage (upper image) and target recognition (lower images).
                
                    Government Accountability Office/GAO
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Government Accountability Office/GAO
    

   
   The Pentagon is building weapons and projects with artificial intelligence capabilities that officials say don't always closely adhere to the agency's own guidelines for AI, according to a congressional watchdog report published in October.   AI researchers and international organizations have long advocated for strict regulation of AI when used in weapons that could become unpredictable or function with little human control, arguing that those tools could endanger the lives of soldiers and civilians and risk quickly escalating wars. But Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has repeatedly dismissed previous caution of AI tools and encouraged rapid autonomous innovation at the Pentagon.   
   The Pentagon issued a memo in January saying the department would become "an 'AI-first' warfighting force across all components, from front to back." Last month, Hegseth announced a new warfare command focused on autonomous weapon development, including drones.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth arrives on stage for a discussion during an annual Army meeting on October 14, 2026 in Washington, DC.
                
                    Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images North America
    

   
   The watchdog report, published by the U.S. Government Accountability Office on Oct. 14, grants a rare look inside how those kinds of projects are being developed.   The GAO surveyed 10 officials involved with building 10 weapons and tools for the Pentagon that use AI to automatically identify targets on the battlefield, process surveillance and improve tactical decision making, and other tasks. The projects are among more than 300 being built with AI in the Pentagon.   When responding to the GAO survey, six of the 10 officials said their teams had "identified risk(s)" with using the projects "in an operational environment."   To address some of those sorts of risks, in 2021, the Pentagon sent a memo outlining six basic tenets to ensure that weapons built with AI are created responsibly. Those six guidelines mainly stress the importance of Pentagon-wide oversight, verification and "real-time monitoring" of the technology, and cooperation with allies "to advance global norms grounded in shared values."   Alissa Czyz, who directed the GAO review, said the tenets evolved from earlier ethical principles, and while they weren't rules, they were understood to be important by people involved with building AI tools at the Pentagon.   
   "It's a memo, right, at the end of the day, so it's not a department instruction," said Czyz. "It's something that the department has signaled that should be implemented."   Most of the people involved with making the 10 weapons and projects reviewed by GAO had taken "at least initial steps" to follow the six tenets outlined in the memo, according to the report, and some of the projects were in early stages, Czyz clarified.   But some of the responses indicated officials weren't always closely following the guidelines.   Four officials told the GAO that requirements for the weapons and projects they were working on weren't "aligned with Responsible AI tenets." And three of the 10 officials told the GAO they "don't know" if the projects will be continuously monitored after they're deployed, though the six tenets encourage monitoring.   
   Officials told the GAO that more access to expertise about the agency's guidelines or staff who know about them would increase their ability to incorporate AI responsibly. But the group that helps manage education on the Pentagon's guidelines, the Department of the Responsible AI Division, is understaffed. Although the group was authorized to hire 10 people in 2023, as of February, only three of those positions were filled and the Pentagon "is unlikely to fill vacant positions or increase staffing," the report states.   "That's a very small number of folks tasked with a large responsibility of responsible AI throughout the department," said Czyz.   The GAO issued two recommendations: The Pentagon should more clearly outline the responsibilities and meeting schedules of the office charged with overseeing AI regulation, and address understaffing. Although the Pentagon agreed with those recommendations, as of Oct. 22, the agency had not implemented those changes, a GAO representative confirmed to NPR.   NPR asked the Pentagon when it planned to make those changes, but did not receive a response.   
   When delivering a speech at SpaceX in January, Hegseth indicated he believed AI development at the Pentagon should not be slowed by those sorts of steps.   "Our enterprise currently operates on staffing and committee cycles measured in months and years, and that's unacceptable," said Hegseth. "Military AI is going to be a race for the foreseeable future where the risks to U.S. national security of moving too slowly outweigh the impacts of imperfect alignment."   NPR would like to hear from more people who work with federal agencies or AI companies and have information to share about how agencies are using AI. You can email the reporter of this article, Chiara Eisner, at ceisner@npr.org or contact her on Signal here, username ceis.78.

title: What's behind the early voting surge? It's more than voter enthusiasm, expert says
description:
Voting expert on what early voting trends this midterm cycle could mean
    
            
                
                Transcript
body:
Voting expert on what early voting trends this midterm cycle could mean
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6012308/nx-s1-9975602" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Election workers remove ballots from a drop box outside the polling center at the Silver Spring Civic Building on Oct. 22 in Silver Spring, Md.
                
                    Finn Gomez/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Finn Gomez/Getty Images
    

   
   As of Friday morning, nearly 21 million Americans have already cast ballots in the midterm elections, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, which tracks voting by mail and in person.   But early voting numbers can be misleading. A surge in ballots cast before Election Day doesn't necessarily mean more Americans will vote overall.   That's because many of those voting early would have voted on Election Day anyway, according to Charles Stewart, a political science professor at MIT and founding director of the MIT Election Data and Science Lab.   Stewart told Morning Edition that the increase reflects both voter enthusiasm and the money campaigns are spending to encourage supporters to vote early.   
   "It also kind of reflects the large amount of money that's in this campaign that's going into retail politics, going door to door, and just making sure that supporters are energized," he said.   Stewart also sees changes in how Democrats and Republicans are voting. Democrats still have an advantage in voting by mail, but that gap is smaller than in 2022 as more Democrats shift to early in-person voting. Republicans' slight advantage in early in-person voting could also narrow.   
   What stood out to Stewart was the early voting activity in Maine and Iowa, two states that haven't been major battlegrounds in recent elections. He said the numbers reflect voter enthusiasm and campaign efforts to mobilize supporters in places that haven't seen as much political activity in recent years.   While speaking with NPR's A Martinez, Stewart also discussed whether concerns about the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) and Trump's opposition to mail voting are changing how Americans vote — and why polls still matter, even if they can't predict exactly what will happen on Election Day.   Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.   The digital version was edited by Treye Green.

title: Ex-FBI employees charged with lying to Congress over Hunter Biden inquiries
description: Hunter Biden, son of former President Jo
body:
Hunter Biden, son of former President Joe Biden, seen in July 2024 in Washington, DC.
                
                    Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
    

   
   The Justice Department has charged two former FBI employees with making false statements to Congress in connection with the bureau's investigations into Hunter Biden and his laptop ahead of the 2020 presidential election.   Bradley Benavides and Nikki Floris each face a single criminal count stemming from testimony before lawmakers in 2023. The pair, who held senior positions on the FBI's now defunct Foreign Influence Task Force, both turned themselves in and made their initial court appearance Friday morning in Washington, D.C.   The new prosecution is the latest politically fraught case to be brought by the Justice Department since President Trump returned to the White House. It dredges back up the bizarre saga surrounding former President Joe Biden's son, Hunter Biden, and his various legal troubles that featured throughout the 2020 presidential campaign.    
   Hunter Biden's laptop was the subject of intense scrutiny after The New York Post reported weeks before the 2020 presidential election that the device was abandoned at a Delaware repair shop in 2019, and then obtained by President Trump's former personal lawyer Rudy Giuliani.   Republicans have long accused the FBI of mishandling the laptop and the investigations into the younger Biden. Hunter Biden was convicted of federal gun charges and later pleaded guilty to separate tax offenses. (Joe Biden signed a full and unconditional pardon for his son in December 2024.)   
   In a statement on X, the U.S. attorney for Washington, D.C., Jeanine Pirro, said Floris and Benavides "allegedly lied to Congress about their roles in the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations, with one claiming they only learned about it from Wikipedia — despite evidence showing their involvement in helping shape the public narrative about Hunter Biden's laptop right before the election."   Prosecutors charged Benavides and Floris by criminal complaint, which means prosecutors have yet to secure an indictment from a grand jury. Under the second Trump administration, grand juries in the nation's capital and other cities have refused on several occasions to return indictments in high-profile, politically charged cases.   At a court hearing Friday morning, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui noted that both of the defendants have "sparkling backgrounds" in federal law enforcement and were longtime dedicated public servants. He also noted that charging them by criminal complaint for conduct that is "quite old" is unusual.   
   Court hearing planned next week   Benavides, 56, and Floris, 46, are due back in court for a preliminary hearing on Tuesday.   In a statement, Floris' attorneys called her a "patriot" who served as "dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years."   "Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It's no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election," they added.   
   The Post reported Hunter Biden's laptop showed wrongdoing by then-Democratic nominee Joe Biden, who subsequently won the election. Some of the data on the laptop was later ascertained to belong to Hunter Biden. House Republicans subsequently launched an impeachment inquiry into President Biden, focusing on Hunter Biden's business dealings at the time his father was vice president. But no evidence has ever been presented that Joe Biden financially gained from his son's business activities.   The complaint alleges that Benavides and Floris both had real-time knowledge of the Hunter Biden investigations, including into his laptop, in their top posts on the Foreign Influence Task Force.   But in interviews with the House Judiciary Committee in 2023, both of them allegedly lied about their knowledge and involvement in those investigations.   Those purported false statements were material to the committee's investigation, the complaint says, because they allowed both Benavides and Floris to "escape" further questioning about Hunter Biden, which hindered the panel's investigation.

title: Ohio could decide control of the Senate. Its rural voters might decide the winner
description: Chris Gibbs, a cattle farmer in rural Oh
body:
Chris Gibbs, a cattle farmer in rural Ohio, says he's been in a deficit for almost three years.
                
                    Keren Carrión/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Keren Carrión/NPR
    

   
   At the weekday farmers market in Athens, Ohio, colorful vegetables are on display for patrons to purchase, community members interact with each other and vendors and one another. It feels like most people in attendance know one another on some personal level.   For a small town like Athens, the farmers market is a gathering place.   "Our Saturday markets have been fully at capacity," said Paige Walters, the Athens farmers market promotions manager.   Athens, Ohio is home to Ohio University. The city is, like many college towns, pretty liberal. But that's not the case in most of the Appalachian communities in the region.   
   Walters noticed that this year, for the first time in a while, the Athens County Republican Party has set up a table at the market.   "I think that does speak to the political climate right now – that it's pretty competitive," she said.   Despite its past as a swing state, Ohio is now considered to be reliably Republican. This election is a little different. With toss-up races for governor and U.S. Senate, Democrats have a chance to win statewide.   But if Democrats want to win, they have to capture voters who voted for Republicans in the past. That includes the rural Ohio voter base, which historically leans conservative.   While rural voters nationwide have voted red in the past (they backed Trump in 2024 by 40 points), recent polling has shown his approval rating in rural America dropping dramatically amid high inflation, tariffs and the war in Iran.   Democrats are trying to gain ground in the unexpected areas. That's especially true in the competitive Senate match up between Sen. Jon Husted, the Republican nominee, and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown as both candidates invest in outreach to rural parts of the state.   "There's a lot of people in rural Ohio that are not happy, whether it's gas prices, diesel prices, the tariffs, the war," Matthew White of Athens told NPR at the farmers market.   
   Affordability top of mind   Multicolored bell peppers, onions and squash line the table at the Cowdery Farms booth. While the weekday market usually has slower foot traffic, farmer Larry Cowdery sold a good amount of produce.   He owns a small vegetable farm along the Ohio River in Long Bottom. There are two big concerns at the top of Cowdrey's mind. The first is the cost of healthcare.   "The big, big issue that we run into is since we're self-employed, we have to find health insurance somewhere," he told NPR. "It's going to be much more expensive next year."   Healthcare premiums on the Affordable Care Act marketplace are expected to increase by roughly 15% in Ohio, in part because of the expiration of federal subsidies. Republicans, including Husted, voted to eliminate the subsidies under the Trump-backed "One Big Beautiful Bill." As a result of sticker shock, Ohio saw the biggest drop — tied with Oklahoma for the most in the nation — in the number of people enrolled in the marketplace last year, with a nearly 33% decline in enrollment.   Cowdery's second concern is the survival of his multigenerational family farm. It's becoming too expensive to run. He said the cost of electricity and gasoline is a big factor. Plus, he relies on fertilizer to grow his vegetables.   "I'm not convinced we're even going to be able to get fertilizer next year," Cowdery said.   That's because of the war in Iran. Most of the nitrogen used in fertilizer travels through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping channel in the Middle East controlled by Iran. Travel through the Strait has been volatile.   As a result of the healthcare and business hardships, Cowdery isn't keen on voting Republican this year. He added that he hasn't been happy with the Republican-led Ohio legislature for the last few years and he doesn't like Husted, either.   
   "I don't trust Jon Husted at all. I think he's a crook," Cowdery said.   Dean Ferrell is at the farmers market chatting with people and milling around the market. The 62-year-old man, a lifelong resident of Athens, said the cost of gas, utilities and groceries have become burdensome. He has had to cut back on buying certain foods because he can't afford it.   "I mean, who would ever thought you'd be paying ten bucks a pound for ground beef? That used to be filet mignon prices, not ground beef," he said.   
   Ferrell tried to look on the upside of his financial reality. Since he's older, Ferrell said he doesn't eat as much as he used to, so he can save some money that way. He added that he wishes politicians could spend "a week or two living like I do."   "Their attitude would be a lot different. I mean, I gotta save money wherever I can, buy reduced and on sale items," Ferrell said. "There's very few things that I pay full price for. You got to, to survive."   Ferrell considers himself to be an independent. While he hasn't decided who to vote for the Senate, Ferrell said he is leaning toward Husted. He doesn't like the direction the Democratic party is headed.   "The far left has basically hijacked the Democrat Party," he said.   A farmer's frustration   On a crisp fall day in rural central Ohio, farmer Chris Gibbs climbs into his John Deere utility terrain vehicle, setting out to survey his land.   "It started in 1983 on our own with $2,500, a pickup truck and a two-year-old daughter," Gibbs said with a chuckle. "So we built that up to 560 acres."   Gibbs, a first generation farmer in Shelby County, grows corn, soybeans, alfalfa hay and has a few dozen cows.   Farming is a tough industry at the best of times. Farms are at the behest of market fluctuations, domestic policy, international relations and mother nature. Tack on high fuel and fertilizer prices, along with Trump's tariffs and the cost of production exceeds the profit.   
   Sitting in his huge combine that used to harvest corn and soybeans, Gibbs said the diesel fuel to run the machinery has increased 50% under the Trump administration and the war in Iran. He fills up the combine about seven times during the harvest season.   "I think about 150 gallons at $7 is $1,000, and that'll run a day and a half," Gibbs said. "That'd be $7,000 worth of diesel fuel."   Politically, farmers tend to vote Republican. Gibbs was one of those Republicans at one point. In a past life, he was the chair of the Shelby County Republicans. He voted for Trump in 2016.   "I'm looking at certainly, buyer's remorse," Gibbs said about voting for Trump.   Gibbs couldn't stand behind Trump's character, his persona on the global stage or the punitive tariffs he said hurt "United States of America's soft underbelly," referring to agriculture. He moved away from Trump in 2018.   Now, in 2026, Gibbs is the chair of the Ohio Democratic Party Rural Caucus and he wants to send Democrat Sherrod Brown back to the Senate.    Brown, Gibbs argued, has the experience necessary to represent rural Ohioans at the federal level.   "We're going to get Sherrod Brown across the line. I have complete confidence in that," Gibbs said.   No career politicians   At a Republican Party event in Guysville, Melissa Jant said she doesn't want a career politician representing her in Congress and that's exactly how she views Brown.   "I absolutely do not want Sherrod Brown back in there. He was there for 30 years. We saw the policies that he put in place. He ran the country down. He ran Ohio down. We just need new blood in there," she told NPR.    
   Her displeasure toward Brown isn't just because he is a Democrat. Some voters view him as the establishment, despite not being a lawmaker anymore.   Jimmy Williams of Monroe County feels similarly. He said Brown was voted out and shouldn't try and head back to his old stomping grounds. Instead, Williams views Husted as the anti-establishment candidate, despite the fact that he is a sitting senator.   "He's a first-term senator there, and he hasn't even been in there long enough to do everything that they're saying on television," Williams said about ads aimed at Husted. "And people need to be smart enough to look through that."   
   Bob Rouch, of Washington County told NPR he is optimistic that Ohio will stay Republican. He believes Trump has done a lot of good for the county and "it's Ohio's responsibility to keep up with that." If Democrats win control, Rouch thinks they won't doing anything aside from target Trump.   "We're going to have these damn investigations, these attempted impeachments and all the baloney that we went through," he said, referring to the last time Democrats controlled Congress while Trump was president.   Williams argued preserving Republican control of Congress is the goal right now.   "America is at risk," Williams said.

schema.headline: Ohio could decide control of the Senate. Its rural voters might decide the winner

title: Gen Z is 'in the thick' of high housing costs. These candidates aim to solve it
body:
Left: Democrat Olaleye Onikuyide, 28, is running for state representative in Connecticut. Right: Republican Lukas Schubert, 21, is campaigning for reelection as a state representative in Montana. Both candidates are focusing on a lack of affordable housing in their states.
                
                    Raquel C. Zaldívar and Sarah Mosquera for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Raquel C. Zaldívar and Sarah Mosquera for NPR
    

   
   WEST HARTFORD, Conn. — "My bus is running slightly behind," Olaleye Onikuyide texted ahead of our meeting at a coffee shop on West Hartford's main street. The 28-year-old Democrat running for Connecticut state representative still made it on time and said he loved riding public transit.   
   Onikuyide also lives with his parents, though he said that's by choice to save money, unlike the many young adults who can't afford to live on their own.   Still, as part of a generation that faces record-high housing unaffordability, he started obsessing years ago over how to make it cheaper. Now that the cripplingly high cost of both rent and homes has become an urgent national conversation, he likens it to being a fan of a niche music group before everyone else caught on.   
   "All of a sudden, it's blown up and everybody's at the concerts and you're like, 'OK, this is a bit of a crowd here now,'" he said with a broad smile.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Onikuyide and his campaign manager, Karo Shakhnazarov, canvass in West Hartford, Connecticut.
                
                    Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
    

   
   Nationwide, housing costs are a top issue for voters in a midterms season laser focused on affordability. A chronic housing shortage has pushed up prices, and the fallout cuts across generations.    
   Younger people are renting with roommates into their 30s. They're struggling to save for a down payment and wondering whether it even makes sense to buy, given today's sky-high prices. Empty nesters looking to downsize can't find an affordable place to go, and longtime homeowners are reluctant to move at all, given current high mortgage rates.   Generation Z candidates from both major parties said their age group has a lot at stake and is uniquely positioned to help create solutions for everyone.   "We're in the thick of it," Onikuyide said, citing not only high housing and gas prices but also student loan debt and a tough labor market. "We might be the generation that is more educated and yet worse off than our parents."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Onikuyide leaves information about his campaign at a voter's home in West Hartford. He appreciates the national debate on high housing costs but says the action to address it is happening at the state level.
                
                    Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
    

   
   His policy goals include creating more mixed-income housing and walkable cities. Adding density to urban areas can be controversial, as longtime residents worry about more traffic or strained infrastructure. But Onikuyide and others also see an opportunity for bipartisanship. And if elected, he would feel well-placed to make life less expensive for his constituents.   
   "I keep one eye on the national conversation about it," he said, "but the action is happening at the state level."   "The experience of being a renter"   About an hour away in New Haven, Conn., 26-year-old Eli Sabin found a quiet room for talking inside the ornate City Hall. He's also a Democrat running for state representative, and he has worked in this building.    When he was a sophomore in college, he started serving on the Board of Alders. That's "our old-fashioned term for the city council," he explained. "We changed some of the zoning rules to allow for denser development and more affordable units."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Democrat Eli Sabin, 26, is running for state representative in Connecticut. He feels his experience as a renter is important, since elected officials at all levels in the U.S. are overwhelmingly homeowners.
                
                    Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
    

   
   Elected officials at all levels in the U.S. are overwhelmingly homeowners. Sabin said it makes a difference that he is a renter, like about 70% of residents in this city.   "I think it's the experience of being a renter and just the insecurity and instability that you feel," he said. His lease is up in May, and he has no idea whether the rent will go up or whether the landlord will even allow him to stay.   
   He would like more protections against eviction and would also like to make it easier to buy a home.   Older people have told him how they bought 30 years ago on a teacher's salary but could never do that today, while younger people feel "pushed out of the community." Some have moved to states such as Texas, Tennessee or Florida, "not because that's where they have the best job opportunities or where they want to be, but because simply that's the place they can afford," he said.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                New Haven resident James Fripp Jr. (left) speaks with Sabin.
                
                    Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
    

   
   Sabin won a three-way primary, beating both a democratic socialist and a longtime incumbent first elected more than a decade before he was born. "I think people feel like we need fight right now," he said. "We need energy, we need new ideas and we can't accept that the status quo is all right."   
   Like Onikuyide, he credited New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani for igniting political energy around tackling the everyday cost of living. But Sabin also pointed to Republican-led states such as Texas and Montana as role models for bipartisan legislation on housing affordability.   A market gap in starter homes   In Kalispell, Mont., Republican Lukas Schubert is only 21 and campaigning for reelection as a state representative. "I'm not even recently the most youngest," he laughed. The state allows people to run for office at age 18.   On Schubert's campaign website, housing is at the top of the issues page, along with Christianity and taxes. "It is a top priority among Republicans as well," he said "It's not just, you know, a Democrat issue."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Montana state Rep. Lukas Schubert, a Republican, hangs a campaign sign in Kalispell. He says homeownership is critical to building wealth, and he wants to create more starter homes that people can afford.
                
                    Sarah Mosquera for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Sarah Mosquera for NPR
    

   
   Home prices in Montana jumped sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic as more people moved there. Gen Z and millennial lawmakers were part of a push to overhaul zoning and red tape. A 2023 package of laws dubbed the "Montana Miracle" aims to make it easier and cheaper to build housing.   
   Those changes are rolling out, but the housing challenge remains vast. Schubert would like to rein in large foreign corporations that buy up homes and noncitizens who own large parcels of land and property but don't live in the state. He also sees a big gap in the market.   "Seemingly all of the new development is apartment buildings or big, you know, 5, 10 million-dollar mansions," he said. His main focus is on starter homes, either single family or duplexes. "That's what we need to be really getting rid of government barriers to producing."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Schubert (left) speaks with voter Mark Shropshire in Kalispell.
                
                    Sarah Mosquera for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Sarah Mosquera for NPR
    

   
   This past session, Schubert proposed a major tax break for developers that sell a newly built starter home for less than 85% of the local median value. It did not pass, but he plans to try again to boost homeownership.   "That has been one of the biggest factors in wealth retention and development for the middle class in this country," he said.   
   Like the Democratic candidates in Connecticut, Schubert wants to keep the American dream alive for new generations.

schema.headline: Gen Z is 'in the thick' of high housing costs. These candidates aim to solve it

title: Military reinforcements move to Mideast. And, millions of Americans vote early
description:
US Prepares For Possible Strikes, Midterm Early Voting, Trump BBC Deposition
    
            
                
                Transcri
body:
US Prepares For Possible Strikes, Midterm Early Voting, Trump BBC Deposition
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-149514/nx-s1-mx-6013298-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Heavier fighting in Iran could resume in the coming weeks as military reinforcements arrive and some U.S. personnel leave the region. This shift comes as a person briefed on the U.S. and Israel's war planning told NPR that the countries were preparing plans for a possible attack on Iran after the U.S. midterms. Iran said it is prepared.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Traffic in Tehran on Wednesday moves past an installation depicting butterflies forming the Iranian national flag.
                
                    Atta Kenare/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Atta Kenare/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   🎧 There are clear signs of preparations for a possible attack, NPR's Greg Myre tells Up First. The U.S. is deploying a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recently visited Israel to meet with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. President Trump will likely consider military action after Nov. 3 to avoid a spike in oil prices before the midterm elections. In response, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Iran is ready for both diplomacy and war. While the U.S. and Israel possess the power to inflict heavy damage, Iran shows no signs of making significant concessions, Myre says. Instead, it demands formal control over the Strait of Hormuz and the withdrawal of U.S. troops from the region.   
   Although Election Day is more than a week away, almost 21 million Americans have already voted, either by mail or early in-person voting, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab.   🎧 That number of votes so far is a lot and is an increase of about 2 million since yesterday, according to NPR's Saige Miller. In key battleground states, early voting is significantly higher compared to the last midterm election. While the early voting data should not be overinterpreted as a predictor of final results, it shows Democrats voting at higher rates than Republicans, Miller says. Unaffiliated voters are also participating early. Democrats are generally more likely to vote early, and Republicans are more likely to turn out on Election Day, Miller says.➡️ A federal judge in California is limiting the Department of Homeland Security's pre-election field operations. The agency says they aim to identify noncitizens who allegedly voted illegally in nine states.➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.   Trump must sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation case against the BBC, a federal magistrate judge ruled. Trump is required to comply with court rules or face sanctions, the judge said yesterday. The case centers on a Panorama broadcast from late October 2024, which allegedly edited the president's Jan. 6 speech to make it appear he incited a violent siege of Congress. Trump has described the broadcast as false, misleading and defamatory under Florida law.   
   🎧 It's unclear if Trump will sit for a deposition after he previously canceled for "matters of national importance" and suggested January as an alternative, NPR's David Folkenflik says. The case initially focused on the economic harm the broadcast posed to Trump's brand and financial prospects. Although the BBC apologized for the splicing, it now seeks to understand Trump's mindset during his testimony, as he may have intended to encourage violence. BBC attorneys say more than 200 defendants from Jan. 6 said Trump's speech motivated them. The BBC is actively pursuing details about how Trump has profited since regaining the White House, most likely to assess the extent of the damage he faces, Folkenflik says.   Deep dive   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        Julianna Conley/NPR
    

   
   Trump promised to lower grocery prices in his second term. While some individual items have gotten cheaper since he returned to office, overall grocery prices have risen, driven by factors such as increased labor costs, tariffs and higher energy prices due to the conflict with Iran. Specific issues facing a single crop, animal species or geographic region can cause the price of one item to rise well above inflation, while lowering the price of another. NPR analyzed five everyday food items — ground beef, eggs, coffee, butter and chocolate chip cookies — to better understand the math behind grocery store prices.   🍔 Ground beef prices have skyrocketed, reaching $6.79 per pound last month, which is an 85% increase over the past decade, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This surge is largely due to weather and financial pressures on producers.🥚 Prices for eggs fell to $2.27 per dozen last month. Outbreaks like the avian flu can cause significant price fluctuations. In March 2025, the average dozen reached a record high of $6.23.🧈 In September, a pound of butter averaged $3.96 — down 17.3% from last year. U.S. butter production has surged as dairy farms expanded their herds and boosted milk supply for popular items like Greek yogurt. This has resulted in an oversupply of butter.🍪 Chocolate chip cookie prices hit a record $5.35 per pound this January, and last month dropped by 20 cents. The price spike is partly due to factors affecting the sweet treat's ingredients, such as higher flour costs driven by the war in Ukraine.☕ The U.S. imports 99% of the coffee it consumes. Severe weather and climate change have affected harvests, and the price of coffee is still 44% higher than it was two years earlier, despite Trump removing tariffs on the product.   
   Read more about why these prices have fluctuated here.   Weekend picks   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Petter Mattei portrays stars in the Metropolitan Opera production of Lincoln in the Bardo, adapted from George Saunders' surreal novel about the president grieving the loss of his son in the midst of the Civil War.
                
                    Karen Almond/Metropolitan Opera
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Karen Almond/Metropolitan Opera
    

   
   Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:   🍿 Movies: A new film version of Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility focuses on the Dashwood family's two oldest sisters, Elinor and Marianne, who face financial insecurity due to laws that disadvantage widows and daughters.   📺 TV: Actor Sharon Horgan stars as Alex, a 50-year-old divorcée who finds herself at multiple personal and professional crossroads in HBO's new show Youth.   📚 Books: Barbara Trapido's Brother of the More Famous Jack follows Katherine Browne, who is determined to escape her stiflingly conventional upbringing and create a life with fewer constraints.   🎵 Music: NPR's New Music Friday host Stephen Thompson breaks down the best albums released today, including Anderson .Paak and Cordae's Heavy Is the Crown and Fenne Lily's Win Win. Listen to a playlist of the best songs from the new albums.   🎭 Theater: Missy Mazzoli's music brings George Saunders' Booker Prize-winning novel, Lincoln in the Bardo, to life in a stage adaptation at the Metropolitan Opera House in New York. Mazzoli is the first woman composer to have a world premiere on the Met stage.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Karl Bushby, pictured here in Turkey in 2025, started his Goliath Expedition 28 years ago.
                
                    Karl Bushby
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Karl Bushby
    

   
   British adventurer Karl Bushby set out from Chile with the goal of walking an unbroken path to his hometown in England. After 28 years, he has returned to the U.K. and plans to return to his mother's home in Hull by Nov. 1.At least four Trump merchandise stores closed this year as the MAGA Mall reports sales fell 30% from his presidential election years.In this week's edition of Far-Flung Postcards, NPR's Carrie Kahn recalls feeling the rare power of nature at Iguazú Falls on the Brazil-Argentina border. A rain-soaked October brought near-record water volumes crashing over the cliffs.   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: A D.C. park was made 'for the pleasure of the people.' Trump's plan would change that
description: Locals rally against Trump's potential r
body:
Locals rally against Trump's potential redevelopment of East Potomac Park at a protest in early October. Runners, cyclists, birders and more worry they will lose access to the park under Trump's plan to overhaul the municipal golf course.
                
                    Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   WASHINGTON, D.C. — President Trump's express wish to take over the East Potomac Golf Links has thrust a municipal D.C. golf course into the national spotlight. But locals rely on that area for much more than golfing — and worry the district could lose an invaluable recreational oasis.   The southern tip of East Potomac Park, known as Hains Point, is beloved by cyclists, runners, picnickers and birders for its waterfront views, cherry trees and Ohio Drive, the scenic three-mile loop around its perimeter. Runners use the wide, flat road to train; it's even a fixture of several major race courses, including the Marine Corps Marathon on Sunday.   
   "It's such an important part of the fabric of this region, even though it's not very well known [beyond it]," said Elizabeth Kiker, the executive director of the Washington Area Bicyclists Association. She herself took her now-husband on a bike ride on their second date 20 years ago.   Locals describe Hains Point as a rare public resource in D.C. It's easily accessible from the National Mall yet removed from the crowds, full of people but free of traffic. Congress created it in 1897, "to be forever held and used as a park for the recreation and pleasure of the people."   And yet, under the president's proposed golf course redesign, Hains Point as people know and love it may cease to exist.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                East Potomac Golf Links and Hains Point as seen from the top of the Washington Monument this week.
                
                    Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Trump said on Truth Social last weekend that renovations would keep the entire park closed for 15 months starting in November. But it's not clear what would be left when it reopens: The rendering he posted shows an 18-hole course spanning the entire peninsula — including the current playground and picnic area on its southern tip — with no road visible around the perimeter.   The White House referred NPR to the Department of the Interior, which did not respond to NPR's questions about whether those features would be removed as part of the redesign. The proposed renovations have so far been the subject of mixed messages from the administration: Trump said last weekend that work would begin in mid-November, then "immediately." But government lawyers said in court Monday that they were not aware of a final plan.   
   Even so, the government abruptly downed hundreds of trees on the course with little warning earlier this month, which critics worry was a pretext for beginning renovations. (The government says it was following up on recommendations from a 2019 landscaping report.) Judge Ana Reyes held a hearing on Monday to learn more about the tree-clearing and decide whether to block further work on the golf course.   But it's not just the golf course that's at stake, as a group called Hains Point Runners told Reyes in the courtroom and a written brief. In its 35-page brief, the group says federal law requires the National Park Service to identify and consider the "longstanding recreational uses of the Hains Point corridor" and ways to avoid harming those uses, before embarking on any work that would change it.   
   "From the perspective of the running community, that did not occur here," lawyers wrote.   Ashley Hawkins of Prince George's County, Md., runs at Hains Point every day, even in the snow. She especially loves the river view and people watching: the families with fishing poles, binocular-wielding birders, people taking a leisurely drive.   "Running is so tied to my mental health," Hawkins said on a recent sunny morning, stretching before she hit the road. "And no place in this area has given me the peace that Hains Point has."   Hawkins has been following the headlines about her beloved running route. While she says she's still in denial about its potential closure, she sees the prospect as part of a pattern of Trump "bypassing" courts to advance his construction projects.   
   "But to me, this feels the most egregious, because he's taking away public space and trying to make it private," she says. "It feels like one of the more king-like things that he's done so far."   Trump's proposal would combine the park's three historic — and historically affordable — courses into one 18-hole "championship-style" course, which has already raised concerns about who will be able to play on it. Trump has said on Truth Social the golf course will "be open to the Public" while also able to host "world class tournaments" such as the U.S. Open and PGA Championship. He's called the current course "dilapidated, and of no further use or effect," dubbing part of it "Trash Island."   
   What's at stake   Each spring, when D.C.'s iconic cherry blossoms bloom, Hains Point is a fan-favorite viewing spot for both locals and tourists. The annual Credit Union Cherry Blossom 10-mile run takes roughly 20,000 participants around the peninsula for that very reason.   
   But race organizers are looking into backup options for next year given the rumored renovations, event director Rob Wolfe told NPR.   In an email to prospective runners earlier this year, the organization said both the proposed golf course renovations and Trump's planned arch on nearby Arlington Memorial Bridge could significantly alter the course. It urged people to share their concerns with lawmakers and the National Park Service.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Hains Point is part of the course of several major road races, including the Credit Union Cherry Blossom ten-mile run each April and the Marine Corps Marathon every October.
                
                    Andrew Harnik/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrew Harnik/AP
    

   
   Wolfe said the best race experience includes as many cherry blossoms as possible — ideally the ones that frame the park. But, he says, the park's future is "more important than our Sunday in April or Marine Corps Marathon's Sunday in October."   "It's really important that people understand that if this roadway goes away, hundreds, thousands of people on a daily basis would lose out," he said.   Luke Cancilla, a runner and physical therapist who works primarily with endurance runners and cyclists, said Hains Point is a particularly safe environment because there are fewer obstacles such as traffic, stoplights and sidewalks. He often recommends it for people who are starting out or returning after an injury.   "It's open to all of us, which makes it so unique," he said. "You don't have to have an experience level … or be intimated to go out there."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The park is a popular spot for fishing in the Potomac River.
                
                    Andrew Harnik/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrew Harnik/AP
    

   
   Summer Delehanty, an avid birder, found out about Hains Point when she moved to the area for work about a year ago. She said it's played a huge role in building her D.C. community.   "I've only been here a year, but I still have so many fond memories of going there," she said. "I was there January 1st looking for the snowy owl … I've been there on super hot days, I've picnicked there."   
   Delehanty has spotted all kinds of birds at that park, including rarities such as the fork-tailed flycatcher. She said Hains Point is a uniquely great birdwatching spot in the district because of its position right along the Potomac River: People have a 360-degree view of the migrating birds that fly overhead or take shelter in the trees.   "There's nothing else in D.C. like it," she said, adding that she's not sure where regular birders would go instead. They could perhaps get similar views from the Virginia side of the river, she said, but those wouldn't count as D.C. bird sightings.   
   The Trump administration cut down 430 of the park's trees earlier this month, with less than a day's notice. That means fewer places for tired birds to rest, Delehanty says, and potentially fewer birds stopping by altogether. And, if the park is closed to humans, there won't be anyone there to track the species that do, which she said is important for conservation purposes.   María-Elena Montero, president of the D.C. Bird Alliance, says the potential closure of Hains Point would mean a "devastating loss of habitat" for birds and humans alike.   "It belongs to the people," she said. "And to lose that aspect of being able to experience such a gorgeous space right in the middle of the city, right in the shadow of an airport and monuments … is a big loss for everybody."   How people are mobilizing   Last October, the Trump administration started dumping debris from another controversial construction project — the demolition of the White House East Wing — on the grounds of the golf course. In February, the D.C. Preservation League and two local golfers sued the government in an effort to stop what they describe as an unlawful takeover of a public course.   
   Fear and confusion grew this summer, when Trump was photographed touring East Potomac with a group including golf course architect Tom Fazio and staffers holding rolled-up renderings. Trump later announced that Fazio would design a new championship-level course, with work set to begin on September 1.   When Delehanty saw that news, she realized "this involves me directly," she said. She decided to put her design skills and sizable social media following to use, designing "Hands off Hains" T-shirts to raise awareness and money for the D.C. Preservation League. She says she's sold around 200 so far, raising about $1,500.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                President Trump and officials toured the East Potomac golf course in June, fueling locals' concerns that construction would soon begin. Trump said this week that work would close the park starting in mid-November, though a plan has not been finalized.
                
                    Mark Schiefelbein/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Schiefelbein/AP
    

   
   "In the grand scheme of things, against an administration, is that going to do anything in court? Not really," she said. "But for me, it's about [the fact] these are 200 people that care so deeply about this they're willing to … wear a shirt, show up to these events and say 'This is not something I'm happy about.'"   
   The push to protect the park is grassroots – and growing.   There's Save East Po, a nonprofit started by a resident named Alex Rosen who works as a consultant and described himself to NPR as "just a guy who really likes a park and doesn't want to see its fundamental characters change significantly, especially without any public input."   The D.C. Bird Alliance is leading a series of daily "Hold the Point!" bird walks next week. And the Washington Area Bicyclists Association has held several installments of a combined bike-ride rally called "Hains Point Hoopla."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                East Potomac Park is a fan-favorite spot for locals and tourists alike to enjoy the cherry blossoms each spring.
                
                    Alex Wong/Getty Images

   The most recent Hoopla, held earlier this month, featured speakers including David Hearn, the former Olympian falsely accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool — and an avid cyclist.   Critics see a throughline in Trump's D.C. construction projects.   "It goes to this overall theme of potentially taking away from the local communities, making things a little bit more challenging and having us modify things in order for something that no one really asked for in the first place," said Cancilla, the running coach.   
   He's one of many who would like to see more input from the community about the changes to East Potomac. Critics of Trump's plan say there are steps the government can take to improve the park — such as adding benches and fixing the crumbling seawall — without risking access to public resources.   Amidst the court battle and confusion, locals are at least heartened to see their beloved park getting more national attention. At a time when its future feels out of their hands, they're encouraging people to speak up and show up.   That's no problem for Hawkins, who says she plans to keep running at Hains Point every day "until they physically tell me that I can't come anymore." Where would she go then?   
   "I'm not ready to answer that question," she said. "I feel really tied to this place."
